items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My predecessors were, first, Nat Hentoff, who after all is an old mentor of mine.

ctx.x: We were going to pick up with your enrolling in Brandeis without your knowledge.

I came in the middle of the academic year. I had gotten out of the Army in January. So right after the winter break I arrived at Brandeis. It was very small then. The first class had just graduated. That was the class of 1952. They had just graduated the previous fall. It was still very small, about 700 undergraduate students, and a great faculty. I quickly made some friends. I was older. I’m 24 now, right? Yes, I’m 24. Of course that was a little more than the average age certainly of incoming freshmen, but…

There was no jazz instruction at Brandeis, needless to say. It had a very good music department, with an all-star faculty of Harold Shapiro and the very gifted, excellent composer, who died very young, named Irving Fine. The titular was Leonard Bernstein, who came in once a week. He was known as the airborne professor, because he flew in from New York to give a lecture which was attended by practically everybody, because he was a brilliant lecturer. We decided – this small core of jazz fans – that since there was…

items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” ... Nat Hentoff was also in it.

ctx.x: Okay. Well I’m going to — in the time I have then I’m going to leapfrog ahead, but only a little bit. Because I wanted to ask you about young Dan goes to Harlem. And I had heard a radio interview that you did, about going up to Harlem and checking out the music and stuff. I wonder what — can you describe like what a night would be like?

Well this was not too terribly long after I came to New York and I had met this little underground trumpet player named Matt Lorber, nickname was “Face”; he knew everybody and everybody knew him, and also met a very hip young lady who was the first to take me to the Apollo Theater in Harlem, and that actually turned out to be a night when Dizzy’s big band was appearing there with Chano Pozo, so I got to see that, which was tremendous. The Apollo was — one thing of course — the Apollo was frequented to some extent…

going, but it wasn’t what it used to be. But there were little clubs and there was this wonderful trumpet player and singer named Hot Lips Page. Lips was my friend, Nat was a kind of protégé of Lips’. Lips was from Texas and he didn’t call him “Face” but he called him “Shorty” which was pronounced “Shouty” — that was his Texas accent. And going to Harlem, Lips lived there, was a wonderful experience. There were after hours places, and the after hours places could be somebody’s apartment where there was an old…

items.title: Hentoff Nat — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Eventually Dan Morgenstern and all that. Yeah, there was a lot of that. ... I can’t speak for Dan and the others. ... they knew me. They knew what I wrote. If we had disagreements, we talked them out.

ctx.x: Let’s talk about your peers as a writer in the early 1950s. Was there a sense of community with – eventually, when people came to New York, like Martin Williams and/or the others – Whitney Balliett, these people who you had historic collaborations with?

Yeah. Once I read Martin, I knew I was in the presence of somebody I had to learn from. Same thing with Whitney: nobody was ever able to put the music into words without being precious or self-exalted, etc., and he also had very good ears. I liked him. He was – both – Martin, and there was a guy named Hsio Wen Shih who wrote very well historically. Yeah, there was some camaraderie. Marshall Stearns was part of that scene, come to think of it. Eventually Dan Morgenstern and all that. Yeah, there was a lot of that.
So you’re saying that it’s the Village Voice column is when you began to expand your written topics outside of just jazz music.
